The big ones:

- The DSM, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, put out by the American Psychiatric Association. The current version is DSM-5-TR. It covers the psychiatric disorders.
- The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines, now in its fourteenth edition. It is about medication, and it is written for people who work in hospitals.
- The Oxford Handbook of Neurology, and the Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry. These are written for doctors and students, and they are dense.
- The Merck Manual, which is free online in several languages.

If you tell me which disorder you have in mind, I can point to the best chapter or the best single source for it.

One thing to keep in mind. A handbook tells you what a disorder looks like and how to treat it. It does not tell you what a particular person will go through. The people who wrote these books learned from patients in hospitals, and often from the families who cared for them. If you are reading one because of a diagnosis, I would read it alongside a doctor who knows the case.

turns.user: List the changes and continuities in television throughout the decades of 80's, 90's and 00's
turns.assistant:
The three decades run from the launch of the MTV video channel in 1981 to the end of the decade when Netflix started sending out its DVD rentals by post, in 2007. Most of what follows holds for American television, which is the tradition I know best. The British picture is sketched at the end, since it overlaps with the American one and diverges in places.

Start with what stayed the same. The basic shape of a season did not change. A show still ran for about twenty-two minutes, with the last few minutes given over to commercials, and a season still ran for about twenty-two episodes. The same was true of the old arrangement, which had three networks, a handful of stations that answered to them, and a ratings company that counted who was watching. The people who ran television still trusted the same thing above all else, which was that a show had to earn its next episode. And the old habit of making people wait still worked. A season still ended on a cliffhanger, and people still talked about it for a year.

Now the changes, decade by decade.

The 1980s began with cable still being a trick of the airwaves. The Federal Communications Commission had ruled in 1972 that cable systems could not carry the networks' own signals, and that rule held until 1987. So for most of the decade, cable was a separate world. It carried sports that the networks would not carry, movies that had not yet been on television, and a music video channel that launched in 1981 and became a force in its own right by the end of the decade. The VCR arrived in the same years. By 1985 there were more players in American homes than there were television sets, and the famous Betamax case reached the Supreme Court in 1984. For the first time, people could record a show and watch it later.

The 1990s began with the Fox network, which launched in 1986 and was still finding its feet. Fox did not need to copy the other three. It could buy old movies and old shows cheaply, and it could take risks that the others would not take. Its first hit, Married... with Children, was a sitcom about a family nobody liked much. Its second, The Simpsons, began as a short on a variety show and became the most watched cartoon on television. Fox also bought the rights to National Football League games in 1994, and that money paid for the rest. Cable had its own boom. The Disney channel launched in 1983, Cartoon Network in 1992, and Nickelodeon made cartoons for older children that the others would not make. In 1996 the cable news channels began covering a presidential campaign from start to finish, and cable news had been on the air for eleven years.

The 2000s began with the DVD player, which reached about a third of American homes by the middle of the decade. People could now skip the commercials, and the people who ran television noticed at once. The same decade brought the remote control with a channel up and a channel down button, and people began to leave a show alone only when they were bored with it. The number of channels had grown so large that nobody could count them

turns.user: What are spherical roller bearings and where are they used?
turns.assistant:
A spherical roller bearing is a rolling-element bearing that can take heavy loads and still run true when its shaft bends a little or sits out of line. Its rollers are shaped like a section of a sphere, and the outer ring has a curved raceway. That shape lets the rollers tilt inside the bearing, so it self-aligns. It also carries load in both directions along the shaft, which is why you'll often see them called double-row or two-row bearings.

Where are they used? Anywhere a shaft carries a heavy load and might bend under it. That includes paper machines, where long rolls of paper have to stay perfectly aligned, and steel mills, where the loads are huge and the environment is rough. You'll find them in mining and aggregate equipment, in heavy industrial fans and blowers, in large pumps and compressors, in crushers and mills, and in wind turbine main shafts, which are long and flex under load. They're common in any heavy industry where a misaligned shaft would fail.

The tradeoff is that they're more expensive than most bearings, and the self-aligning action means there's a little extra friction. So they're usually specified where the load or the misalignment justifies the cost.

The name covers a range of designs. Some are built for very heavy loads, some for high speeds, and some for harsh conditions like dust, water or heat. The basic idea is the same in all of them.

turns.assistant:
Start with the spec. The current version is USB 4 version 2.0, from June 2021. Earlier versions are still in use, so read them too: 3.2, 3.1, 2.0. The Type-C connector is in the USB Type-C Specification, which is a separate document. Get the official spec from the USB Implementers Forum, or the free preview.

Read the connector chapter first. Type C has 24 contacts, laid out so the plug can go in either way. The orientation is detected by two configuration channels, CC1 and CC2. One pin, VBUS, carries power. The rest carry data.

Then learn the roles. A port can be a host, a device, or a dual-role port that can be either. A host supplies power on VBUS. A device draws it. The CC pins also carry sideband signals, which let connected devices talk to each other without going through the host.

Then learn the lanes. USB 3 and later use two differential pairs, one for sending and one for receiving. USB 2.0 uses a single pair. The same four data pins carry both, so a USB 3.0 cable has more conductors than a USB 2.0 cable.

Then learn the speeds. 1.5 and 12 megabits a second for USB 2.0. 5, 10 and 20 megabits a second for USB 3. The numbers are raw. Real throughput is lower, because of framing and overhead.

Then learn the power side. The power delivery protocol, which runs over the CC pins, lets devices negotiate voltage and current. A charger and a laptop talk over CC, and so do two peripherals that want to share power.

Then learn the alternate modes. Type C can carry signals that are not USB at all, such as DisplayPort, HDMI or Thunderbolt, if the host and the cable both support them. The host decides which mode a lane runs in.

Then learn the cable ratings. A cable is rated for a current, a data speed and a video mode. A cheap cable may be rated for 3 amps and USB 2.0 speeds. That is fine for a phone charger. It will fail as a laptop cable, and the failure can be a laptop that will not charge.

Then learn the faults. Mismatched speeds are the common one: a USB 3.0 host plugged into a USB 2.0 port, or a USB 2.0 device on a USB 3.0 host. The devices usually work together at the slower speed, which is how the fault hides. Then there are cable faults, such as a missing CC connection, which makes a dual-role port unsure of its own role. And there is the orientation problem. Because the plug works either way, the receiver has to work either way. Early receivers did not, and the host had to guess which way round the plug was.

Then practice. Read a data sheet for a Type C controller, such as a Texas Instruments or a Microchip part. Compare it with the spec. Read a cable vendor's test reports. Build a small project, such as a host that enumerates devices on a bus, or a Type C port that reports its state on the CC pins.

turns.assistant:
Here are six, each with the core idea and one puzzle it makes possible.

1. Echo. You can record ten seconds of yourself, then a ghost replays your inputs while you act alongside it. The twist: it replays your button presses, not your path, so if the level has changed since you recorded, the ghost goes somewhere else. Puzzle: record yourself jumping at a wall, then move a crate so the same jump lands the ghost on a switch you can't reach.

2. Living in shadows. You can only stand on shadows. Every light source casts shadows, and some platforms only exist where shadows overlap. Puzzle: two lamps whose shadows separately cover half a gap, so you have to find the one spot that joins them.

3. Ink. You draw platforms with a limited ink supply, and ink only stays down where it's shaded. Puzzle: you have to draw a bridge in the dark, then find a light source to hold it up while you cross.

4. Heavy pockets. Everything you pick up adds weight. You're light enough to be blown by wind and pulled up by balloons, and heavy enough to sink in water and crack weak floors. Puzzle: carry three stones to crack a floor, then drop them in the water below to float a crate across.

5. Fold map. The level is a sheet of paper. At crease lines you can fold it, bringing distant platforms on top of each other. Puzzle: fold the left half over so a ledge lands next to you, cross, then unfold with you on the far side.

6. Two characters, one mind. You play both a thief and a guard at once, and every input runs both of them. The guard can open doors the thief can't, and the thief can pick locks the guard can't. Puzzle: the guard walks into a room to stand on a pressure plate while the thief, somewhere else, picks the lock on that room's door.

A few things are worth knowing before you pick one. The first thing is the one input. Every game here works because the player has one control and the idea gives it depth. If you find yourself adding a second button, the idea is probably doing less than it should.

The second thing is the tutorial. Each of these needs a room where the player learns it by doing, and the best level in the game is usually the first room done well.

The third thing is what you're good at. A game about shadows is mostly lighting and collision, which is a fair first project. Echo needs recording and replay, which is a fair first project too. If you'd rather spend your time on writing, a game about a library where every book is a door might suit you better. That one's about a librarian who can read any language, and the puzzles come from books that describe rooms you haven't reached yet.

Which of these appeals to you, and what are you building it in? I can help with either.

These companies try to ensure advertisers can reach their audience while publishers maximize their revenue. And, these companies can be categorized as DSPs, SSPs, MMPs, Mobile Ad Networks & Mediation Platforms and they all have different functions. For example, SSPs connect app developers and publishers with advertisers, while DSPs allow advertisers to manage their ad buying across various exchanges and publishers. 
Also, with the help of MMP companies such as Adjust, Kochava, we have solutions for tracking ad performance, user acquisition, and user's in-app behavior. The data we are getting from MMPs allow us to optimize campaigns for better ROI. 

In addition to these companies, we have Mediation platforms that help app developers integrate and manage multiple ad networks within their apps. The most well known Mediation companies are Unity(Ironsource) and Applovin Max.

turns.assistant:
You have the main pieces right. A few points are mixed up, and one of them matters a lot if you are building a product on this data.

What each player does

- SSP (Supply Side Platform). The publisher's side. An app or site owner connects their ad inventory to an SSP, which sells it to buyers, usually through an auction. Example: PubMatic, Xandr.
- DSP (Demand Side Platform). The advertiser's side. An advertiser uses a DSP to bid for inventory across many exchanges and SSPs from one place. Example: The Trade Desk, DV360.
- Ad network. A middleman that buys ad space in bulk, often at a fixed CPM, and resells it. Publishers use them when they have no other buyer. They are still important, especially for smaller publishers, but they sit between the two sides.
- Mediation platform. A tool the publisher integrates into their app. It calls several ad networks and SSPs at once, lets them bid against each other, and takes a cut. Example: AppLovin MAX, Unity (Ironsource), Google Ad Manager.
- MMP (Mobile Measurement Partner). A third party that tracks installs, in-app events and revenue across campaigns from different networks. Example: Adjust, Kochava, AppsFlyer, Branch.

Where your text goes wrong

1. "SSPs connect app developers and publishers with advertisers." That is not quite right. The SSP connects the publisher to the buyers. The advertiser connects to the buyer through the DSP. The SSP does not connect directly to advertisers.

2. "The standout players are Unity, IS, Mintegral, Admob, Verve, Liftoff, Google Ad Managers etc." These are not all the same kind of player.
   - Unity and Ironsource are mediation platforms.
   - AdMob and Google Ad Manager are Google's ad server and mediation tools.
   - Liftoff is a DSP (an advertiser tool).
   - Mintegral and Verve are ad networks.
   Calling them all "mobile ad networks" blurs the line between buyer and seller, and that line is the whole point of the ecosystem.

3. "Unity and IS are dominating the market thanks to their mediation platforms." Unity and Ironsource are big because they own mediation, a big ad network, and (in Unity's case) a game engine. That gives them inventory, buyers and data in one company. That is worth knowing. It does not make them an ad network in the old sense.

4. "The maybe the most important player is Mobile Ad Networks." Important for whom? For a small publisher with no direct deals, yes, the networks fill the gaps. For a big app, the real money is usually in direct deals and programmatic through an SSP. And the big mediation companies are also buyers, which is where the conflict can come in.

The data you get from MMPs

You are right that MMP data is what lets you optimize for ROI. But keep two limits in mind.

- An MMP sees what happens after the click. It does not see what the ad showed, who saw it, or what the bid was. If you want to understand why a campaign did well or badly, you need the ad network's or SSP's data too.
- Privacy rules and platform changes have made MMP data less complete than it used to

The other problem is that you're building the set from the first exon, but the group's range is `start` and `end`, which come from the transcript as a whole. If the first exon doesn't reach `start`, your set says it does, and that's a bug waiting to happen. Pull the exon out of `exons` by its coordinates, or rebuild the set from the exon list itself. If you go that way, remember that `extend` takes an iterator of references, so write `group_exons.extend(exons.iter())`.

One more thing. The `any` closure borrows `acc` mutably, and the loop also borrows `acc` mutably when it pushes a new group. Rust won't let you hold both at once, so move the `push` outside the `any`, or collect the new groups in a temporary and push them after the loop finishes.

turns.user: Does it violate the Categorical Imperative if a government tries to force their culture upon an automatous region that is under their jurisdiction but maintains its own unique culture traditions and practices?
turns.assistant:
It can, depending on what the government is doing. The Categorical Imperative gives us two tests that are useful here.

First, ask whether the maxim could be a universal law. Could we will that any state may force its culture on a distinct people within its borders whenever it chooses? If every state acted on that principle, no minority culture would be safe anywhere, not even the culture of the majority in some other state. That kind of world is one you could not consistently will, because you yourself might belong to a minority somewhere. So a policy of forced assimilation fails this test.

Second, ask whether people are treated merely as means to an end, or also as ends in themselves. When a government compels a region to abandon its language, its dress, its religion or its customs, it uses that people as material to be reshaped for the government's own purposes, such as unity or control. It does not respect their capacity to choose how to live. That fails this test as well.

There is a straightforward exception. If the government is enforcing a law that protects people's rights, it is not violating the imperative. For example, if a local tradition involves a practice that harms people, such as forced marriage, the state may prohibit it. That is the same duty it would have toward anyone else. The Categorical Imperative does not require a state to tolerate everything.

The tension is real. A state must be able to enforce its laws everywhere, and that sometimes means restricting certain practices. But forcing people to think, worship and live like the majority is something else. Kant himself was uneasy about the idea of a state enforcing virtue, and he thought moral improvement had to come from individuals.

So the line is between enforcing rights, which is required, and erasing a culture, which is not.

turns.user: Can I be thinner if I refuse to have breakfast?

Maybe, but it isn't a reliable way to get there, and it isn't the way most people manage.

Skipping breakfast can mean you eat less overall that day, especially if you're not hungry in the morning. Some studies find that people who skip breakfast eat fewer calories by nightfall. Others find they make up for it later, or that they're hungrier and choose less healthy food. The results vary a lot from person to person.

There are other reasons to be careful. If you skip breakfast and then eat a large lunch, your blood sugar and insulin rise more sharply than if you'd eaten something small in the morning. Task
My task was to help the team bring order to that flow: make the work visible, give the team a clear way to decide what to do next, and keep urgent requests from swamping everything else.

Action
- Introduced Kanban, with a shared online project board so everyone, inside and outside the team, could see the state of the work.
- Set work-in-progress (WIP) limits so the team finished things before starting new ones.
- Defined a clear Definition of Ready (DOR) and Definition of Done (DOD) for each item, so work entered and left the board on agreed criteria.
- Named a single Product Owner to own prioritisation, giving the team one clear source of priorities.
- Added a monthly retrospective, borrowed from Scrum, to adjust the way of working as we learned.

Both turn a 1D ECG trace into a 2D time-frequency image that you can feed to a CNN. They differ in how they slice time and frequency.

Short-time Fourier transform (STFT)
- What it does: slides a fixed window along the signal, takes an FFT of each window, and stacks the results.
- Output: a spectrogram, usually shown as magnitude in dB with a colormap.
- Resolution: fixed. The window length sets a tradeoff. A short window gives good time precision and poor frequency precision; a long window does the opposite.
- Frequency axis: linear in Hz, which matches how the ear and most audio work, but ECG isn't audio.
- Speed: fast with the FFT.
- Good for: beats that are fairly steady, like sinus rhythm or regular tachycardia.

Continuous wavelet transform (CWT)
- What it does: correlates the signal with one wavelet shape, stretched and squeezed to many scales. Small scales are short wavelets; large scales are long ones.
- Output: a scalogram.
- Resolution: variable. Short wavelets pin down when something happens; long wavelets pin down what frequency it is. This matches the ECG well, because a QRS complex is brief and high frequency while the ST segment is slow.
- Frequency axis: roughly logarithmic. Scales map to frequencies through the wavelet's centre frequency and the sampling rate.
- Speed: slower than STFT, especially at fine scale resolution.
- Good for: transient events, arrhythmias, beats that change shape.

Which to choose
- If your task is beat classification with mostly clean, regular beats, STFT is usually enough and trains faster.
- If you need to catch brief abnormalities, or your data is noisy, CWT often gives better results.
- Try both on a small holdout set. The difference is often small, and the data decides.

Optical Lines: Fundamentals and Advantages

1. Introduction

An optical line is a communication path that carries information as light. The light travels through a medium such as glass or plastic, and at each end of the path a transmitter turns electrical signals into light while a receiver turns the light back into electrical signals. Most optical lines today are fibres, thin strands of glass about the thickness of a human hair, but the term also covers free-space links through the air or through vacuum, such as the laser links between satellites.

Optical lines are the backbone of modern communications. Under the oceans they carry the great majority of intercontinental traffic. On land they connect cities, districts and individual buildings. At the scale of a data centre they connect servers and storage. The advantages are large: very high capacity, very long distance without repeaters, immunity to electromagnetic interference, and security that rests on the laws of physics.

This report explains how optical lines work, the main kinds of optical line, and why they are advantageous. It is written for readers with some technical background. Wherever possible the explanation begins with the physical principle, then gives the practical form, and finally states the advantage that follows.

2. The physical basis

2.1 Light as a signal

Light is an electromagnetic wave. Its colour is described by its wavelength, the distance between successive peaks, or by its frequency, the number of peaks that pass a point each second. In optical fibres the usual wavelengths are around 1,310 nanometres and 1,550 nanometres, in the near infrared. Visible light runs from about 400 to 700 nanometres.

Information is put onto the light by changing some property of it. The simplest method is to turn the light on and off, one state for a binary 0 and another for a binary 1. This is called intensity modulation. More advanced methods also change the phase of the light, or its polarisation, or use several wavelengths at once. At the receiving end a photodiode absorbs the light and produces a current proportional to its intensity, so the original electrical signal is recovered.

2.2 Total internal reflection

The reason light can travel long distances through a glass strand is total internal reflection. A glass core is surrounded by a cladding of glass with a slightly lower refractive index. When light travelling in the core reaches the boundary at a shallow angle, it is reflected back into the core instead of passing into the cladding. The light bounces down the strand, staying inside the core for kilometres.

The difference in refractive index is small, typically a few percent. In single-mode fibre the core is about 9 micrometres in diameter, and in multi-mode fibre it is larger, typically 50 or 62.5 micrometres.

2.3 Attenuation

As light travels, some of it is lost. The main causes are absorption, in which the glass turns light into heat, and scattering, in which tiny irregularities in the glass send light out of the core. The loss is measured in decibels per kilometre. In modern single-mode fibre at 1,550 nanometres the loss is about 0.2 decibels per kilometre. At 1,310 nanometres it is a little higher, around 0.35

- x and y are points, usually in a plane or in space. Think of them as positions.
- ||x − y|| is the distance between them, the ordinary straight-line distance you learned in geometry.
- σ (sigma) is a positive number. It sets the scale. Think of it as the width of the bell.
- K(x, y) is a number between 0 and 1.

If you stand at x and look at y, the kernel gives you a number that tells you how close y is to you, on a scale from 0 (very far) to 1 (right here).

Property 1. It is always positive.

K(x, y) > 0 for every pair x, y. Nothing here can go negative. The exponential function never touches zero; it only gets closer and closer. This matters because in many applications the kernel is treated as a weight, and you cannot give something a negative weight and call it a weight.

Property 2. It depends only on the distance.

K(x, y) = f(||x − y||) for some function f. If you slide both points by the same amount, the value does not change. If you move x and y apart, the value drops, and it drops smoothly. There are no bumps, no dips, no surprises.

Property 3. It is symmetric.

K(x, y) = K(y, x). The distance from x to y is the same as the distance from y to x. This seems obvious, but it is worth saying, because not every useful function has it.

```

turns.user: What are spherical roller bearings and where are they used?
turns.assistant:
A spherical roller bearing is a type of rolling-element bearing that can take heavy radial loads and some axial load, and can still run properly even if the shaft bends a little or the housing isn't perfectly aligned. It does this because the outer ring has a curved raceway, and the rollers are shaped like a barrel. The barrel shape lets the roller tilt slightly inside the raceway, so misalignment doesn't force the parts to rub against each other.

They are used wherever there is heavy load, some misalignment, or both. Common places include:

- Heavy machinery such as mining and construction equipment, crushers and mills
- Paper and steel mills, where loads are heavy and the environment is dirty
- Large electric motors and generators
- Rolling mills and other metalworking equipment
- Ship and vehicle propeller shafts
- Any shaft that is long and supported at both ends, where the two supports may not line up perfectly

They are usually mounted in pairs, facing each other, so the assembly can take axial load in both directions.

The trade-off is that they are larger and more expensive than simpler bearings, and they are not suited to very high speeds.

Start with the big picture, then work down to the details. The USB system is a stack: the physical layer, the electrical layer, the protocol, and the host and device software. Type-C is mostly a physical connector, but it changed how power and data share the cable, and it added a sideband channel for configuration.

Begin with the USB 2.0 baseline. Learn the four wires: VBUS (power), D+ and D- (differential data), and GND. Understand single-ended signaling, pull-up resistors on the device side that tell the host which speed it is, and how the host enumerates a device by reading its descriptors. If you know this, most of the USB 3.0 and Type-C material will make sense.

Then move to the Type-C connector itself. It is 24 pins in a small, reversible plug. The extra pins carry alternate mode signals, power negotiation, and a configuration channel. Learn the pinout, the CC pins and their pull-down and pull-up resistors, and how the plug detects orientation.

After that, study the power delivery side. Type-C uses the CC line to negotiate voltage and current between the source and the sink. Learn the roles: source, sink, and dual-role port, and how a port can switch between them.

Then learn the data lanes. USB 3.0 and later use two differential pairs for 5 Gbit/s and above, plus the original USB 2.0 pair for backward compatibility. Learn how the lanes are mapped in a Type-C cable, and how the connector handles orientation.

Once the hardware is clear, study the protocol layers. The transaction layer handles packets, endpoints, and transfers. The link layer handles enumeration, addressing, and error recovery. The host controller interface, such as xHCI, is how the operating system talks to the USB hardware.

Finally, learn the software stack. On Linux, the core is the USB subsystem in the kernel, with drivers for host controllers, devices, and class drivers like mass storage, HID, and CDC. On Windows, it is the USB stack in the kernel and user-mode libraries. On embedded systems, you may use a USB device or peripheral controller library.

Use these resources in order. The USB-IF website has the specifications, starting with the Type-C connector document. The USB 2.0 specification is the best place to begin. For a readable overview, look at the book "USB Complete" by Jan Axelson. For the deeper layers, "USB 3.0 and Beyond" by the same author covers the later versions. The Linux kernel documentation and the USB-IF developer site have practical guides.

Practice by building something small. A USB 2.0 device on a microcontroller, such as a virtual serial port or a HID device, will teach you the enumeration process. turns.assistant:
They care enough to block it, and often enough to ban you. Most ISPs have acceptable use policies that forbid using their network to attack anything, and a lot of them enforce that. They can see the traffic, and they can stop it. Some will warn you, some will cut you off, and some may pass your details to the authorities. It's not just a theoretical risk. In the US, for example, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act makes attacking computers without permission a crime, and that includes attacking your own network through someone else's devices. The same kind of law exists in most countries.

If you want to test your own network, do it in a way that keeps other people out of it. Isolate the machines you're testing on, or run the test inside a lab that doesn't touch the internet. Then you won't run into the ISP, and you won't run into the law.

Isolation and Ingenuity: The Making of a Man in Robinson Crusoe

Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) is usually remembered as the story of a man who survives shipwreck on a deserted island. The story is indeed about survival, but it is also about what kind of man the island makes of him. Crusoe begins as an ungrateful young man who disobeys his father and runs to sea. He ends as a sober, providentialist colonist who owns the island and rules it. The island does this through hard labour, through sickness, through the discovery of a footprint, and through the arrival of Friday. This essay argues that Defoe makes his point by letting the reader watch a man change: by giving a plain, dated account of practical work, by showing how fear and faith compete in the mind, and by turning the island into property.

The first thing the reader sees is the labour. Defoe gives page after page of plain numbers: how many bushels of rice Crusoe hauls in, how long it takes to make a pot, how many attempts it costs to get a boat seaworthy. The plainness does the work. The reader feels the weight of the tasks because the narrator does not pause to comment on them. He simply reports that it took him more than two months to cut the wood and shape the hull, and that after ten months he could launch it, though it lay too far from the water to use. The boat becomes a measure of his character. He sets out with courage, but he lacks patience. Once he has learned to work slowly and carefully, he begins to own the island. This is the first turn in his change. A man who can count his days and measure his wood is no longer the same man who ran to sea at nineteen.

The second turn happens inside him. At the start of his twenty-fourth year on the island, Crusoe falls ill, dreams of a man descending from a hill with a spear, and wakes convinced he is about to die. That night he prays for the first time in years, and soon after he recovers. A few days later he finds a two-edged sword hanging by his bed, which he takes as a sign. From that moment he begins to keep a spiritual journal, writing down the good and bad days as if they were a ledger. His prayers are not always simple gratitude. He complains to God, asks why he was left there, and argues with Providence. The island forces him to face himself, and he argues with God as he would with a partner. Later, when he finds a footprint in the sand, his mind runs through every possible explanation: a shipwrecked man, a native tribe, the devil. The fear is real, and so is his habit of looking for a reason. This habit, applied to his own life, is what turns him into a man who reads signs.

The third turn is ownership. Crusoe keeps coming back to the word mine. He calls the island his dominion, his plantation, his kingdom. He has no king to answer to, and he is quick to say so. The island gives him everything he needs, so he does not need anyone else, and this is the loneliness Defoe is most honest about. Once he has named his possessions, he names the people around him too: Caliban, the savage, Friday.

Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) is often read as a story about survival. It is that, but it is more. The island matters less than what Crusoe does with his solitude. The novel's enduring power comes from its steady attention to a man who has been stripped of society and slowly builds a new one, first inside himself and then around him. Its realism makes the transformation convincing, and its religious reflection gives that transformation a shape. ```

    └── days                     (subcollection)
        └── 14                   (document: day, e.g. "14" or "2024-01-14")
            └── orders       (subcollection)
                └── {autoId} (document: order)
                      name:     string   (e.g. "Coffee")
                      quantity: number (e.g. 2)
                      price: number (e.g. 3.5)
```

A full path to one order looks like:

Use the same ID pattern for every level. If you use "01", "02" … for months and "1", "2" … for days, the IDs sort correctly when Firestore lists them.

When you write an order, set its fields with `setData`:

                .collection("days")
                .document(String(day))
                .collection("orders")

```

```swift
func ordersFor(month: String, day: Int) async throws -> [Order] {
    let db = Firestore.firestore()
    let snapshot = try await db.collection("expenses")
                               .document(month)
                               .collection("days")
                               .document(String(day))
                               .collection("orders")
                               .getDocuments()
    return try snapshot.documents.map { try $0.data(as: Order.self) }

What you would need to do is three things at once. You would need a body that mimics human skin, hair and bone. You would need a way to move it with the small, constant adjustments a real body makes. And you would need a face that can form every human expression.

If you want blinking, you would use small motors or shape-memory alloy to close the eyelids, and saline gel to keep the surface moist.

For the face, you would need many small actuators, probably harmonic drives or linear motors, placed behind the skin to pull the cheeks, lift the brows, tighten the jaw and move the tongue. CHAMELEON works by rewriting the class files the game loads. You put your changes in a text file, and CHAMELEON turns that into new .class files that Minecraft runs instead of the originals. To change a mob, you edit its AI in the text file, then rebuild and relaunch.

Here's the usual way to do it.

1. Set up CHAMELEON.

Download it from the official site and put the .jar in a folder. You'll also need the Minecraft version you're playing, and a Java development kit installed.

Run this to unpack the game's class files:

java -jar chameleon.jar unpack -d <minecraft-version>

That creates a folder with the game's classes. Copy the mob class you want to change into a separate "source" folder, and keep the unpacked folder somewhere safe. You'll unpack again after each update, so you don't want to lose it.

2. Write the change in CHAMELEON's format.

The format is plain text. A few rules:

- Every class starts with `class <full name> {` and ends with `}`.
- Fields, methods and inner classes follow the same pattern.
- Comments start with `//` and run to the end of the line.
- To delete something, delete the lines. To keep it unchanged, leave it alone. To add something, insert it inside the class.

Here's a minimal file that changes what happens when a zombie attacks. It keeps everything else exactly as the game has it, and only replaces the attack method:

```
class net.minecraft.world.entity.monster.Zombie {

    // ... everything else from the original class, unchanged ...

    public void attack(net.minecraft.world.entity.LivingEntity p_146674_) {
        // Your code here. For example:
        // p_146674_.hurt(this.damageSources().mobAttack(), 4.0F);
    }

}
```

The `p_146674_` is the target. If you delete the method entirely, CHAMELEON deletes it from the game. If you leave it out completely, it stays as the original.

3. Rebuild.

From the CHAMELEON folder, run:

java -jar chameleon.jar build -s <source-folder> -d <minecraft-version>

If it says "Build successful," new .class files are in the output folder.

4. Launch Minecraft with the new classes.

You need two things: the version you unpacked, and a JVM argument that tells Java to load your folder instead of the game's own copies:

-Dchameleon.loadDir=<path-to-output-folder>

How you do that depends on your launcher. In the official launcher, edit the version, add the argument to the JVM options, and launch. In CurseForge or similar, you usually set it in the profile's Java arguments.

5. Test, then repeat.

Run the game and try the change. If it doesn't work, look at the console. CHAMELEON prints its changes and any errors there, and that's usually the fastest way to find a problem.

Some things to keep in mind.

- Only one version at a time. The classes for 1.

3. Ask the package. If the program came from a package manager, its package may include a completion file:
   - Debian/Ubuntu: `dpkg -L <package>` lists its files.
   - Arch: `pacman -Ql <package>`.
   - Fedora: `rpm -ql <package>`.

4. Ask the project. Project pages and GitHub repositories often have a `contrib/` or `completion/` directory.

_myprog() {
  local cur="${2}"
  COMPREPLY=()
  # Positional arguments
  COMPREPLY=( $(compgen -W 'alpha beta gamma' -- "$cur") )
  # Option flags
  COMPREPLY+=( $(compgen -W '--help --version -h -v' -- "$cur") )
  return 0
}

```

Data flows both ways, but each port has one host controller. Type C adds a third role, the dual-role port, which can be a host or a device depending on which way the cable is plugged in. This is why Type C has an orientation ID, or CC pin.

3. Then learn the pins. Type C has 24 pins. The most important for a beginner are the power pins, the data pins and the CC pins. The power pins carry VBUS and ground. The data pins carry differential pairs: D+, D-, TX and RX. The CC pins are the configuration channels. There are two of them, CC1 and CC2. One pin in the connector is always grounded.

The CC pins are the heart of Type C. A plug has a pull-down resistor on each CC pin. A receptacle has a pull-up, an open circuit, or sometimes a pull-down. When nothing is plugged in, a host looks for the pull-downs. When it finds them, it knows a cable is present and which way it is oriented. The orientation ID is a signal on one CC pin that tells the host which plug orientation it is. If you read the CC section of the spec, the rest of the pinout makes sense.

4. Learn how a connection starts. The host enumerates devices. It sends a setup packet, reads the device descriptor, and assigns an address. Then the device can transfer data. This is the same for Type A, Type B and Type C. The connector does not change the protocol.

5. Learn the alternate modes. Type C can carry non-USB signals. DisplayPort, Thunderbolt, HDMI and charging protocols like Qualcomm's Quick Charge and USB Power Delivery all use the same pins in different ways. The CC pins negotiate which mode is active. Power Delivery uses the CC lines to talk between the source and the sink about voltage and current.

6. Build something small. The easiest project is a Type C to Type A adapter with the CC pins wired correctly. Type A hosts expect a pull-down on the CC line. If you wire an adapter that ignores this, enumeration fails, and the failure tells you more than any diagram. A microcontroller with a Type C controller, or a development board with a Type C port, is the next step.

7. Learn from the failures. The most common mistakes are wrong pin assignments, ignoring the CC pull-up and pull-down, and mixing up TX and RX. When something does not work, check the pinout first, then the CC state, then the protocol.

Here are five, each with the core idea and one puzzle it makes possible.

1. Echo. You can record ten seconds of yourself, then a ghost replays your inputs while you act alongside it. The twist: it replays your button presses, not your path, so if the level has changed since you recorded, the ghost goes somewhere else. Puzzle: record yourself jumping at a wall, then move a crate so the same jump lands the ghost on a switch you can't reach.

2. Living in shadows. You can only stand on shadows. Solid ground burns or crumbles. You carry lamps and breakable mirrors, and every light source casts shadows that become your platforms. Puzzle: angle a mirror so a lamp's beam paints a stepping-stone across a gap, then walk the stone before the lamp burns out.

3. Ink. The level is a blank page. You have a finite ink supply, and every platform you draw costs ink. Some surfaces soak up ink and can't be drawn on. Puzzle: you need three platforms to cross, but only have ink for two, so you draw the middle one, cross, then erase the first platform behind you to fund the last.

4. Fold. The level is a sheet of paper. At crease lines you can fold it, bringing distant platforms on top of each other. Puzzle: fold the left half over so a ledge lands next to you, cross, then unfold, knowing the fold also moves things you haven't reached yet.

5. Tide. You control the water level instead of the character. Platforms are only passable when submerged, dry or exposed, each with a different rule. Raising water connects one path and closes another. Puzzle: raise the water to float a crate across a room, then lower it to leave the crate stranded on a high ledge where you need it.

A few things that help whichever you pick. Pick one mechanic and dig into it rather than stacking many. The best puzzle games teach the rule without a word of text: the first room shows it, the next room tests it, the third twists it. And try to make the fail state cheap. A death that costs five seconds keeps people trying; one that costs a long run makes them quit.

Keep it short and simple. Most of what you say doesn't matter; what you do matters more. But three things help.

First, give your boss two weeks' notice, not one day. Show up on your last day and do your work. That's the biggest thing you can do while you're still there.

Second, tell your boss in person before you email it. Say something like: "Can I talk to you for a minute? I've decided to leave. My last day will be [date]. I'm giving you two weeks' notice, and I'll make sure my work's covered before I go."

Third, don't argue or explain. If your boss asks why, you can say: "It's just what's right for me right now." You don't owe anyone a reason.

And when you hand it in, don't say you're quitting. Say you're resigning. One word sounds more like a decision and less like a mood.

What happens after that is out of your hands. Your boss might get upset, or offer you more money to stay, or ask you to train your replacement. Whatever they do, keep doing your work. If they offer you more money, don't accept it unless you mean to stay. If you take more money and then leave anyway, you've broken their trust.

If this is a job at fourteen, talk to your parents first. At fifteen, most places still require a parent to sign when you quit.
